study.title: Daniel 11 - Conflicts between kingdoms, profanation of worship, and the end of the oppressor
study.overview: Daniel 11 presents an extensive and detailed view of political and military successions that directly affect God's people. The first part describes the Persian period and the ascension of Greece; the second follows the dispute between the king of the north and the king of the south, with fragile alliances and successive wars; the third concentrates on the figure of a wicked ruler who deceives, persecutes the faithful and profane the sanctuary; the latter shows the final arrogance of that king, his advance against the glorious land and his sudden fall, because he limits his end.

outline.title: Persians, Greece and the fall of a great kingdom
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the confirmation that the history of nations is under divine rule. After the Persian period, a very powerful king will arise in Greece, but his kingdom will be broken and divided, not preserved for his offspring. The text highlights the fragility of human power: even the vastst kingdom does not remain as the king imagines.

outline.title: The game of forces between the north and south
outline.explanation: From here, the vision follows the dispute between two rival powers that strengthen, make agreements, marry for convenience and then betray each other. Although they seem to dominate the events, these alliances are unstable and end up in new campaigns, sieges and falls. The people of God appear indirectly, hit by these struggles between empires.

outline.title: The despicable ruler and persecution of the holy people
outline.explanation: A king emerges who receives no legitimate honor, but takes power by mistake and uses cunning, intimidation, and false alliances. He profanes the sanctuary, interrupts the continual sacrifice and tries to ward off many of the covenant. Still, those who know God resist, and the wise teach others, even suffering, with suffering serving for refinement and purification.

outline.title: The final arrogance and its decreed end
outline.explanation: The last section extends the figure of the arrogant king, who exalts himself above all gods, honors military forces, and redistributes lands by interest. At the time of the end, he advances with violence, strikes many nations, reaches the glorious land and assembles its tents between the seas and the holy mountain. But his career ends without human help: he comes to an end because the limit was established by God.

study.context: The chapter places the prophetic look amid the succession of empires that affected Judah and Jerusalem. The notes report that Daniel 11 expands earlier views of the division of Alexander's empire and, in particular, about the period in which the northern and southern kingdoms disputed the region of Judah. The focus of the text is not just political: events are narrated because they directly influence the temple, worship and perseverance of the people of God. The notes also associate the expression "great glorious mountain" to Zion, Jerusalem, and the temple, that is, the place God has chosen to make his name dwell.
study.theology: Theologically, Daniel 11 teaches God's sovereignty about history. Kings rise, make agreements, conquer and lose territory, but none escape the limit set by God. The text also shows that fidelity to the covenant can bring suffering, and that political and religious pressure reveals who really knows God. Opposition to true worship does not surprise God; rather, it is included in the revelation to strengthen the faithful. There is still a theme of judgment: arrogant power seems to prosper for a time, but its apparent invincibility ends when the wrath of God is completed and what is determined is fulfilled. At the same time, verses 32 to 35 show that suffering can purify, refine, and make the wisest firmer, so that persecution is not useless before God.

scholarViews.insight: The "Glorious Holy Mountain" includes Zion, Jerusalem and the temple, the place where God chose to make his name dwell; the reference to the sea probably points to the Mediterranean Sea.
The ruler of 11:21 is interpreted as Antiochus Epiphanius, a fierce enemy of the Jewish religion and persecuting of those who remained faithful.
The "Kytim's on the ships" are understood as Roman power, which interrupted the advance of Antiochus and forced him to retreat.

questions: What does Daniel 11 teach about the difference between apparent human power and God's real government about history?
In what ways do verses about deception and profanation help to discern when political or religious alliances become unfaithful to the covenant?
How can the idea of being refined through affliction strengthen the endurance of the believer today?
study.practice: Read this chapter remembering that political and religious crises do not nullify God's purpose. When there is pressure to negotiate faith, stay firm in the covenant, even if this costs reputation, comfort or advantage. It is also appropriate to cultivate discernment: not all apparent stability is fidelity, and not every immediate victory is divine approval. Apply this by assessing their covenants, priorities, and commitments to God, and encouraging others to remain faithful even in times of confusion.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is highly specific, but the given notes do not explain all the historical details of each verse. In addition, the commented readings identify various elements with particular figures and historical events, but the biblical text itself, taken in isolation, allows only to safely affirm the succession of kingdoms, persecution of the people of God, the desecration of worship and the final fall of the arrogant king. No names, dates or locations have been added other than in the given notes.
